title: Memory in machines: Hopfield networks, replay, attention and transformers (Bridge to AI)
text:
CHAPTER 9. MEMORY
SECTION 9.4. MEMORY IN MACHINES: HOPFIELD NETWORKS, REPLAY, ATTENTION, AND TRANSFORMERS

Why a whole section on machine memory?

This is the dedicated "Bridge to AI" section of the memory chapter. Memory is where the conversation between neuroscience and AI has been especially rich. Ideas flowed from neuroscience to AI (Hebbian associative memory, replay), from AI back to neuroscience (complementary learning systems, attention as retrieval), and in some cases the two fields arrived at the same mathematics from different directions. We will cover four topics: associative memory and Hopfield networks, memory-augmented neural networks, attention and transformers, and the memory architecture of modern AI systems compared with the brain.

Associative memory: content-addressable storage

A computer's memory is location-addressable: to retrieve data, you specify an address, and the memory returns what is stored there. Human memory works differently. You retrieve a memory by providing part of its content: a smell brings back a childhood scene, the first few notes of a song bring back the rest. This is content-addressable or associative memory. Hebb's cell assemblies (section 7.1) and Marr's theory of CA3 (section 9.1) are theories of associative memory in the brain.

Early mathematical models of associative memory were developed in the 1970s, including by Teuvo Kohonen, James Anderson, Kaoru Nakano, and Shun-ichi Amari. The simplest is the linear associator: to store pairs of patterns (key k, value v), set a weight matrix W equal to the sum of outer products of values and keys:

  W = sum over stored pairs of v * k^T

To retrieve, multiply a key by W:

  W * k_query = sum over pairs of v * (k^T * k_query)

If the stored keys are orthogonal and normalized, presenting a stored key returns exactly its value. If keys are not orthogonal, retrieval returns a mixture, with interference. Notice that this weight matrix is built by a Hebbian rule: each weight W_ij is the sum of products of the activities of output unit i and input unit j. Keep this formula in mind; it will reappear in the discussion of transformers.

Hopfield networks

In 1982, John Hopfield, a physicist then at Caltech, published "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities" in PNAS. The paper presented a recurrent network of binary threshold units (like McCulloch-Pitts neurons, section 4.3) with symmetric connections, and it brought the tools of statistical physics to bear on neural computation.

The Hopfield network has N units, each with state s_i equal to +1 or -1. Connections are symmetric (w_ij = w_ji) with no self-connections. To store P patterns xi^1, ..., xi^P (each a vector of +1 and -1 values), set the weights by a Hebbian rule:

  w_ij = (1/N) * sum over mu of xi_i^mu * xi_j^mu

Units are updated one at a time (asynchronously):

  s_i <- sign( sum_j w_ij * s_j )

Hopfield's key insight was to define an energy function:

  E = -(1/2) * sum over i, j of w_ij * s_i * s_j

With symmetric weights and asynchronous updates, each update can only decrease E or leave it unchanged. So the network always moves downhill in energy and eventually settles into a local minimum, a stable state. The Hebbian rule makes the stored patterns local minima of the energy (approximately). If the network is started in a state that is a corrupted version of a stored pattern, it rolls downhill to the nearest minimum, which is usually the stored pattern. This is pattern completion: content-addressable memory implemented by the dynamics of a physical system.

The energy picture is powerful because it connects neural networks to physics. The Hopfield network is mathematically related to the Ising model of magnetism and to spin glasses. Using methods from statistical physics, Daniel Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund, and Haim Sompolinsky showed in 1985 that a Hopfield network with N units can store about 0.138 * N random patterns before retrieval breaks down catastrophically; above that load, the network enters a "spin glass" state where memories are no longer retrievable. So a network of 1,000 units can store about 138 random patterns. This limited capacity, linear in N, was seen as a major limitation.

Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, with the Nobel committee citing Hopfield's associative memory network and Hinton's Boltzmann machine (a stochastic generalization of the Hopfield network that can learn) among their foundational contributions.

Hopfield networks and the brain

The Hopfield network is a simplified model, but it captures ideas that appear throughout neuroscience: attractor states as memories (section 9.2, working memory; section 9.3, continuous attractors for head direction and grid cells), pattern completion in CA3, and energy landscapes as a way to think about neural dynamics. Experimental evidence for attractor dynamics in the brain includes the abrupt switching of hippocampal place cell maps when an environment is gradually morphed from one shape to another, reported by Tom Wills, Colin Lever, Francesca Cacucci, Neil Burgess, and John O'Keefe in 2005, and the ring attractor in the fly's head direction system.

Modern Hopfield networks

In 2016, Dmitry Krotov and John Hopfield introduced "dense associative memories," Hopfield-like networks with energy functions involving higher-order interactions, such as E = -sum over mu of F(xi^mu dot s) with a rapidly growing function F (for example, a high power or an exponential). These networks have much larger storage capacity; with an exponential function, capacity can grow exponentially with N in some formulations. In 2020, Hubert Ramsauer, Sepp Hochreiter, and colleagues extended this to continuous states with an energy based on the log-sum-exp function, and showed that the update rule of this "modern Hopfield network" is:

  new state = X * softmax( beta * X^T * query )

where X is a matrix whose columns are the stored patterns, query is the current state, and beta is an inverse temperature. A single update typically retrieves the stored pattern most similar to the query (if beta is large) or a weighted average of similar patterns (if beta is small).

This is exactly the form of the attention mechanism in transformers, which brings us to the third topic. Before that, a brief detour.

Memory-augmented neural networks

Standard neural networks store knowledge in their weights. In the 2010s, several researchers built networks with explicit, external memory that the network can learn to read from and write to, an idea partly inspired by working memory and by the separation of hippocampus and cortex.

- In 2014, Alex Graves, Greg Wayne, and Ivo Danihelka at DeepMind introduced the Neural Turing Machine, a neural network controller coupled to an external memory matrix, with differentiable read and write operations using attention over memory locations. It could learn simple algorithms such as copying and sorting sequences.
- In 2016, Graves and colleagues introduced the Differentiable Neural Computer, an improved version that could, for example, learn to answer questions about graph structures such as a transit network.
- Memory Networks, introduced by Jason Weston, Sumit Chopra, and Antoine Bordes at Facebook in 2014, used a memory of stored sentences and attention to retrieve relevant ones for question answering.

These systems showed that attention-based retrieval from a memory store could be trained end to end with gradient descent. They influenced, and were then largely overtaken by, the transformer.

Attention and transformers

In 2017, Ashish Vaswani and colleagues at Google published "Attention is all you need," introducing the transformer architecture. The transformer dispenses with recurrence and processes a sequence by letting each element attend to all other elements. The core operation, scaled dot-product attention, is:

  Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q * K^T / sqrt(d_k) ) * V

where Q (queries), K (keys), and V (values) are matrices obtained by multiplying the input representations by learned weight matrices, and d_k is the dimension of the keys. (In this formula the rows of Q, K, and V correspond to sequence positions, which is why it looks transposed compared with the Hopfield update above.) For each position, the query is compared with all keys by dot products; the softmax turns similarities into weights summing to one; and the output is the weighted sum of the values.

Interpreted as memory, each position's key-value pair is a stored item, and each query retrieves a blend of values whose keys match. This is content-addressable memory: a soft version of the associative retrieval described above, and mathematically the same as one step of a modern Hopfield network. The scaling factor 1/sqrt(d_k) plays the role of the inverse temperature beta.

Transformers became the dominant architecture for language models (GPT, BERT, and their successors), and later for vision, speech, protein structure prediction, and many other domains.

Linear attention and fast weights

If the softmax in attention is replaced by a simpler kernel function, the attention computation can be rewritten as:

  output_t = W_t * phi(q_t),  with  W_t = sum over s <= t of v_s * phi(k_s)^T

where phi is a feature map. This "linear attention" (Angelos Katharopoulos and colleagues, 2020) maintains a weight matrix W_t that is updated at each step by adding the outer product of the new value and key: a Hebbian update. As noted in section 6.2, Schlag, Irie, and Schmidhuber (2021) showed that this makes linear transformers equivalent to "fast weight programmers," networks that rapidly write associations into a matrix of fast weights. In neuroscience terms, this is like a synaptic memory that is rapidly modified during processing, reminiscent of short-term synaptic plasticity or rapid hippocampal encoding. Recent recurrent architectures for long sequences (such as various state space models and "linear RNN" variants) use related ideas, sometimes with decay or gating terms that act like forgetting.

Attention and the hippocampus

Several researchers have proposed direct connections between transformer attention and hippocampal function.

- Trenton Bricken and Cengiz Pehlevan showed in 2021 that attention approximates Pentti Kanerva's "sparse distributed memory," a model of associative memory proposed in 1988 that Kanerva had related to the circuitry of the cerebellum.
- As mentioned in section 9.3, Whittington, Warren, and Behrens (2022) showed that transformers with suitable positional encodings relate closely to the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine model of hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, and develop place-cell-like and grid-cell-like representations.
- Others have compared the key-value structure of attention to the hippocampal "index" theory, in which the hippocampus stores keys (indices) that retrieve values (cortical patterns), a theory proposed by Timothy Teyler and Pascal DiScenna in 1986.

These are hypotheses and analogies, not established facts about the brain. But they show how a mechanism engineered for language modeling has turned out to resemble theories of biological memory, perhaps because both solve the same underlying problem: retrieving relevant stored information based on its content.

In-context learning: memory without weight change

Large language models show a remarkable ability called in-context learning: given a few examples of a task in their prompt (for example, several English-to-Mongolian translations), they can perform the task on new inputs without any change to their weights. The examples are held in the context window, and attention retrieves and combines them. This is a form of rapid learning that relies on activity (the context) rather than weight changes, somewhat like working memory, or like the rapid binding attributed to the hippocampus.

Research on how in-context learning works has found specific attention mechanisms called "induction heads," described by Catherine Olsson, Nelson Elhage, and colleagues at Anthropic in 2022, which detect when a token appeared earlier in the context and copy what followed it. This pattern completion mechanism is reminiscent of autoassociative recall. Other studies have shown that transformers trained on certain tasks can implement something like gradient descent within their forward pass, learning from examples in context.

Memory architectures compared

Putting together this chapter, we can compare memory in the brain with memory in modern AI systems built around large language models:

Working memory.
Brain: persistent activity and short-term synaptic changes in prefrontal and other cortex; capacity about four chunks; lasts seconds unless rehearsed.
AI: the context window, holding thousands to millions of tokens; available during a single session; erased when the session ends.

Episodic memory (fast learning of specific experiences).
Brain: hippocampus with sparse, pattern-separated codes; one-shot learning; replay during sleep and rest.
AI: external memory stores and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in which documents or past interactions are stored as vectors (embeddings) in a database and retrieved by similarity to a query; one-shot storage; retrieval by content. Patrick Lewis and colleagues introduced the term "retrieval-augmented generation" in 2020.

Semantic memory and skills (slow learning of general knowledge).
Brain: distributed neocortical networks, learned slowly through interleaved experience and consolidation; procedural skills in basal ganglia and cerebellum.
AI: the model's weights, learned through pretraining on vast datasets with gradient descent; updated by fine-tuning.

Consolidation.
Brain: replay during sleep transfers hippocampal memories into neocortex gradually, interleaved with old knowledge.
AI: periodic retraining or fine-tuning on accumulated data, sometimes mixing in old data to prevent forgetting; experience replay in reinforcement learning; generative replay in continual learning research. Some research systems explicitly "consolidate" information from their external memory into their weights.

Reconstruction and distortion.
Brain: memories are reconstructed at retrieval and can be distorted (false memories).
AI: generated content is reconstructed from learned statistics and can contain confident errors (hallucinations); retrieval augmentation reduces but does not eliminate them.

The gaps

Despite the parallels, important differences remain:

- The brain learns continually throughout life, updating its synapses during every waking moment and every night's sleep, without separate training and deployment phases. Most AI systems learn in large offline training runs and then operate with frozen weights.
- The brain's episodic memory is integrated with the rest of cognition: memories are tagged with emotion, context, and significance, and their storage is prioritized accordingly. AI retrieval systems typically store everything uniformly or according to engineered rules.
- The brain's memory systems are energy efficient and operate with noisy, slow components. AI systems use precise digital memory and large amounts of energy.
- The brain forgets, and forgetting may be useful: it removes irrelevant details, supports generalization, and prevents interference. Designing useful forgetting in AI systems is an active area of research.

Summary

- Associative (content-addressable) memory can be built with Hebbian outer-product weights; retrieval suffers interference when keys overlap.
- Hopfield networks (1982) store memories as energy minima of a symmetric recurrent network and retrieve them by pattern completion; their capacity is about 0.138*N random patterns. Hopfield and Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
- Modern Hopfield networks have much larger capacity, and their update rule is mathematically identical to transformer attention.
- Memory-augmented networks (Neural Turing Machine, Differentiable Neural Computer, Memory Networks) introduced attention-based reading and writing of external memory.
- Transformer attention, softmax(Q*K^T/sqrt(d_k))*V, is soft content-addressable retrieval; linear attention is equivalent to Hebbian fast weights.
- Proposed links connect attention to sparse distributed memory, hippocampal indexing, and hippocampal-entorhinal models.
- Context windows, retrieval-augmented generation, and model weights parallel working, episodic, and semantic memory; continual learning, prioritization, efficiency, and forgetting remain gaps.
